candidate.answerReason: Coupon 1 beats coupon 2 when \(p>200\) and beats coupon 3 when \(p<225\). Only $219.95 satisfies both strict conditions.

methods.label: Method 1: Find the allowable price range
methods.explanation:
Every listed price exceeds \(\$100\), so all three coupons are available. Let \(p\) be the listed price in dollars. Their reductions are, respectively,
\[
0.10p,\qquad20,\qquad0.18(p-100).
\]
The subtraction in the third expression matters: coupon 3 discounts only the amount above \(\$100\).

For coupon 1 to beat coupon 2, we need
\[
0.10p>20,
\]
which gives \(p>200\). For coupon 1 to beat coupon 3, we need
\[
0.10p>0.18(p-100).
\]
Expanding and collecting terms gives
\[
18>0.08p,
\]
so \(p<225\).

Both comparisons must hold, giving \(200<p<225\). The endpoints are excluded because they produce ties. The only listed price in this interval is \(\boxed{\$219.95}\), choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
methods.levelReason: The method uses percentage expressions and two school-level linear inequalities.

methods.label: Method 2: Check the listed prices
methods.explanation:
All five prices exceed \(\$100\), so coupon 2 always saves \(\$20\). Coupon 1 saves 10% of the whole price, while coupon 3 saves 18% of the excess above \(\$100\). We can compare these reductions directly, keeping the percentage calculations exact.

At \(\$179.95\) and \(\$199.95\), coupon 1 saves \(\$17.995\) and \(\$19.995\), respectively. Both are less than coupon 2's \(\$20\), eliminating choices A and B.

At \(\$219.95\), the percentage reductions are
\[
0.10(219.95)=21.995,
\]
\[
0.18(219.95-100)=21.591.
\]
Coupon 1 therefore saves more than both \(\$20\) and coupon 3's reduction.

For the remaining two prices, coupon 3 beats coupon 1:

At \(\$239.95\), their reductions are \(\$25.191\) and \(\$23.995\), respectively.

At \(\$259.95\), their reductions are \(\$28.791\) and \(\$25.995\), respectively.

Thus only \(\boxed{\$219.95}\) qualifies, choice \(\mathrm{C}\).

candidate.annotationRationale: The shared target is forming percentage reductions on the correct amounts, particularly the excess above $100. Percentage conversion supports both methods. Modeling and solving simultaneous inequalities belong to the range method; decimal evaluation and comparison belong to the direct method.
